question: What is Merrill's advisor growth strategy, and how has it changed?

claims.text: Merrill: Merrill grows its advisor force through an extensive training program and through experienced hiring of advisors; approximately one-third of net new households in Q2 2025 were added by newly trained advisors (scope: Merrill and the Private Bank; period 2025Q2).

Merrill: Merrill's core advisor growth strategy is its training program that trains people in wealth management at Bank of America and Merrill; recruiting experienced advisors is also being picked up but is not an enormous part of the strategy (period 2025Q4).

Merrill: Merrill develops advisors through the Advisor Development Program, a structured path that progresses through roles (Client Associate, Financial Solutions Advisor, Financial Advisor) and graduates advisors to Merrill Core Advisor, designed to help advisors build a book of high-net-worth clients (page content as of 2026-11-03).
Merrill: Merrill's foundational belief for its wealth business includes that having the best advisors enables it to deliver exceptional client outcomes.

Merrill: Merrill returned to veteran broker recruiting after largely pulling back at the end of 2017; the firm restored a focus on hiring and a more aggressive offer under Co-Presidents Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf, who took over in 2023, and recruited assets doubled year-over-year.

Merrill: CFO Borthwick describes the advisor growth strategy as continuing to grow the sales force, referencing the 'Merrill 5% guide' of aiming for 5% growth over the next 3 to 5 years, and notes advisor attrition is now at near historic lows (period 2026Q2).

Merrill: CFO Borthwick describes the advisor growth strategy as primarily a training program (training people in wealth management at Bank of America and Merrill), supplemented by recruiting experienced advisors which 'isn't an enormous part' of the strategy (period 2025Q4).

Merrill: Management states they continued to add financial advisors to the sales force in Merrill and the Private Bank through the extensive training program and experienced hiring of advisors (scope: Merrill and the Private Bank; period 2025Q2).
Merrill: Management states they continue to attract talent across both new and experienced advisers (period 2026Q1).
Merrill: Management describes the ability to attract clients and experienced advisers to the platform as part of the growth strategy (period 2026Q3).
Merrill: Management states both Merrill and the Private Bank continued to attract talented advisers drawn to the breadth of the platform (scope: Merrill and the Private Bank; period 2026Q2).
Merrill: Management notes expense growth supported the cost of hiring to add experienced advisors to the platform in Merrill and the private bank (scope: Merrill and the private bank; period 2025Q1).

Merrill: Merrill describes the Advisor Development Program as a multi-stage training path through which participants progress through three roles until graduating to Merrill Core Advisor, a route for growing new financial advisors (page content as of 2026-11-03).
Merrill: Merrill's foundational beliefs state that having the best advisors enables delivering exceptional client outcomes.

Merrill: CFO Alastair Borthwick stated Merrill is picking up recruiting of experienced advisors, but that is not an enormous part of the strategy; the strategy is a training program training people in wealth management at Bank of America and Merrill to drive net new flows (period 2025Q4).
Merrill: CFO Alastair Borthwick stated Merrill co-heads Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf are driving to keep growing the sales force, with adviser attrition now at near historic lows (period 2026Q2).

Merrill: CFO Alastair Borthwick stated Merrill and the Private Bank continued to add financial advisors to the sales force through the extensive training program and experienced hiring of advisors (scope: Merrill and the Private Bank; period 2025Q2).

Merrill: CFO Alastair Borthwick stated the firm remains focused on adviser productivity and long-term client relationships, driving productivity higher on newer and existing financial advisers and continuing to attract talent across new and experienced advisers (period 2026Q1).

Merrill: Merrill executives touted that recruited assets doubled year-over-year as the firm returned to veteran broker recruiting; the firm had largely pulled back from veteran broker recruiting at the end of 2017 but returned after Co-Presidents Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf took over in 2023 and restored a focus on hiring and a more aggressive offer.
Merrill: Management's foundational belief states that having the best advisors enables the firm to deliver exceptional client outcomes.

Merrill: CFO Alastair Borthwick stated expense growth supported the cost of hiring to add experienced advisors to the platform in Merrill and the Private Bank (scope: Merrill and the private bank; period 2025Q1).
Merrill: CFO Alastair Borthwick stated results reflect the firm's ability to attract clients and experienced advisers to the platform (period 2026Q3).

Merrill: CFO Alastair Borthwick stated both Merrill and the Private Bank continued to attract talented advisers drawn to the breadth of the platform and ability to deliver comprehensive solutions for clients (scope: Merrill and the Private Bank; period 2026Q2).
Merrill: Merrill said it had added advisors from Morgan Stanley, Truist and Wells Fargo representing a combined $1.8 billion in client assets.
Merrill: Merrill added a team from UBS (John Vazquez and Manuel Monasterio) with $1.2 billion in client assets.
Merrill: Merrill added a private wealth team managing $1 billion in assets from UBS Wealth Management USA in Boston.
Merrill: Merrill added an advisor managing $205 million at Morgan Stanley and another overseeing $150 million at Edward D. Jones & Co.
Merrill: JPMorgan Chase recruited a Merrill advisor (Tiffany Yu) managing about $940 million in assets, a competing firm taking a Merrill advisor.

Merrill: According to Wolfe Research, Bank of America (Merrill's parent) had the largest net advisor losses this year through Aug. 13 at 552, followed by Edward Jones and Equitable Advisors at 334 each; LPL Financial had the highest net gain at 378, followed by Raymond James at 293.

Merrill: The advisor growth strategy has changed: Merrill largely pulled back from veteran broker recruiting at the end of 2017, but returned to it after Co-Presidents Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf took over in 2023 and restored a focus on hiring and a more aggressive offer, with recruited assets doubling year-over-year as of October 2026; the firm's CFO also frames the strategy as centered on a training program, with recruiting experienced advisors being picked up but 'not an enormous part' of the strategy.

Merrill: Merrill has returned to veteran broker recruiting: the firm largely pulled back from veteran broker recruiting at the end of 2017, then returned after Co-Presidents Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf took over in 2023 and restored a focus on hiring and a more aggressive offer; recruited assets to the wealth unit doubled year-over-year as of October 2026. Why it might matter: the firm's co-heads Lindsay Hans and Eric Schimpf are driving to keep growing the sales force, with adviser attrition at near historic lows (period 2026Q2).

Merrill: Merrill is picking up the recruiting of experienced advisors, but this is not an enormous part of its strategy; the firm emphasizes a training program to train people in wealth management across Bank of America and Merrill (period 2025Q4). Why it might matter: the training program is ultimately what management believes can keep driving net new flows.

Merrill: Merrill continued to add financial advisors to the sales force in Merrill and the Private Bank through its extensive training program and experienced hiring of advisors, with approximately one-third of net new households in Q2 added by newly trained advisors (scope: Merrill and the Private Bank; period 2025Q2). Why it might matter: during the quarter, between Merrill and the Private Bank, the firm added 7,100 net new relationships.

Merrill: The Advisor Development Program (ADP) progresses through roles—Client Associate, Financial Solutions Advisor, Financial Advisor, then Merrill Core Advisor—with licensing (SIE, Series 7 and Series 66) and durations of approximately 13 months for the CA/FSA roles and approximately 1-4 years for the Financial Advisor role (page content as of 2026-11-03). Why it might matter: the program is Merrill's structured path that progresses through roles and graduates advisors to Merrill Core Advisor to help advisors build a book of high-net-worth clients.

Merrill: Merrill continues to attract talent across both new and experienced advisers and is driving productivity higher on both newer and existing members of its financial advisers team (period 2026Q1). Why it might matter: the firm remains focused on adviser productivity and long-term client relationships.

Merrill: Merrill leadership's aim is to keep growing the sales force, and adviser attrition is now at near historic lows (period 2026Q2). Why it might matter: management states they are aiming for 5% sales force growth over the next 3 to 5 years, with more to do despite being off to a good start.
